name: Ross Mountjoy
relocation: Moving to the Aragón region of Spain in November 2026 on a digital nomad visa, so from then on he works from a European time zone.
summary: Self-taught full-stack engineer with over ten years of experience building and scaling web applications, from system architecture and backend APIs through frontend UI and the infrastructure underneath. A robot is what turned it into a career: when Anki released Vector he wrote VectorCloud, a web interface for it, and has been shipping open source since, including DashMachine, which has passed 11 million Docker Hub pulls. The last few years have gone deep on AI: building against the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs, writing MCP servers and Claude Code extensions, and running local models on his own hardware for private inference. Linux has been his daily driver for over ten years.
direction: Open source AI and robotics is the passion, and embedded AI is the goal. He has built assistants that live on hardware in his house rather than in a browser tab, first on a Raspberry Pi and now on a dual-GPU box with on-device speech and a wake word he trained himself. Robots are the future, and open source robots are how we get there. The work he wants is the software around the robot that makes it usable: SDKs, control surfaces, on-device speech and language, the developer experience. He wants to help build the Linux of robotics.

highlights: Stayed on as an independent contractor after four years as a full-time employee; Savi is now the main client of Mountjoy Software Solutions.

Designed and built the Savi AI Gateway solo: a byte-faithful Anthropic proxy with per-product prompt injection, server-side retrieval over Qdrant, full request tracing, an outcome-driven learning loop with offline scoring and human approval, an audited HubSpot proxy and an OAuth 2.1 MCP server. In production within a week of the first commit.
Owns the AWS infrastructure and runs their SAML single sign-on service.
AI engineering, including LLM integration and agent tooling.
Migrated their entire stack off EC2 and onto ECS, containerising a legacy PHP application and modernising the stack around it.
Built a custom SAML identity provider and service provider platform to run single sign-on for their users.
Replaced the DocuSign integration in the core application flow with an in-house PDF generation, signature and faxing system.
Wrote their Bitbucket Pipelines CI/CD, which builds and deploys the containerised stack.
Stood up Qdrant and built semantic search over the help centre articles behind the Savi Assistant, using embeddings and cosine similarity retrieval.
Full-stack development across a PHP, Laravel, Python and React codebase.
Owned the AWS infrastructure, including ECS, ALB, IAM, Cognito, S3 and Route 53.
Sole developer of the web application for a startup turning over $30m+ a year, which was sold to Revive, Inc.
Built and ran the Python, FastAPI and Vue.js codebase end to end.
Served buyers and sellers across the DC Metro area.
Specialised in the business side of the job: graphic design, business systems, online marketing, Google Ads and SEO.
Consulted for other agents in the area on the same things, which is where the software career started.

projects.name: Savi AI Gateway
projects.blurb: One gateway every Savi product points its stock Anthropic SDK at: byte-faithful proxy, per-product prompt injection, server-side RAG, full tracing, and a learning loop that turns customer outcomes into human-approved guideline changes. Sole engineer, in production within a week of the first commit.
projects.details:
Savi had several internal AI products each talking to Anthropic directly: its own key, its own copy of the system prompt, and no shared view of what was being spent or whether the answers were any good. I designed and built a single gateway that every product now points its unmodified Anthropic SDK at. First commit 9 August 2026, v1 in production inside the week, 165 commits and 35 pull requests by mid September, all mine.

**Three surfaces, one Laravel app.** The gateway is a byte-for-byte pass-through of the Anthropic Messages API including SSE streaming; nothing is re-serialised through an SDK, so new betas and content block types pass on day one. Per-key rate limits return Anthropic-shaped errors so client SDK backoff just works, and every request is recorded: model, tokens, duration, stop reason. A React and Inertia console manages apps and keys, prompt profiles, guidelines, the knowledge base, traces, analytics and a playground, with role-based access and mandatory 2FA. An MCP server with OAuth 2.1 and dynamic client registration lets any Savi employee add the company knowledge base to Claude Code or claude.ai with their Google account and nothing else.

**The prompt lives on the key, not in the app.** A request is resolved to a product and surface by its API key and the published system prompt is injected server-side, so apps send a generic completion and never hold prompt text. Non-engineers try the unpublished draft in the playground, then publish globally with one button. Cache breakpoints are budgeted against the caller's own so the injected prefix can never make a request fail.

**Retrieval behind a stock SDK.** PDFs and synced Zendesk help content are chunked and embedded into Qdrant, and search runs as a tool loop inside the gateway: the caller gets one finished answer, and if the model reaches for one of the caller's own tools the loop stops and hands control back. Retrieval policy is set on the app rather than the key, so an internal-only source cannot leak to a customer-facing key by accident.

**A learning layer with a human in the loop.** Products report outcomes after the fact: CSAT, whether a human edited or rejected the draft, what was actually sent. Outcomes mature for five days, weighted by recency and how much a person touched them, and a weekly miner turns the negative tail into proposed guideline changes. Every proposal is scored by replaying past requests offline with the rule applied and having a judge model compare the answers; the score orders the review queue, and approval is the only thing that creates a rule. A second pipeline runs the same idea over roughly 282,000 archived support conversations through the Anthropic Batches API in five idempotent, resumable stages, with older conversations offered a schema that can only produce prose advice so a nine-year-old policy cannot resurface as a rule.

**HubSpot as an audited proxy.** The gateway is the HubSpot base URL for Savi's dashboards. Reads pass, writes are allow-listed per key per object, and a write to a never-before-touched property has to notify RevOps before it clears; a notice that cannot send does not clear the write. The only real HubSpot token lives on the gateway.

Runs on ECS Fargate behind a shared ALB with RDS MySQL, Redis and Secrets Manager, separate staging and production, Bitbucket Pipelines running style checks and the PHPUnit suite on every pull request. No test spends tokens; upstream is stubbed. The MCP tests perform the real initialize handshake, because a test that skips it passes against a server no client can talk to.

The repository is Savi's and private, so there is no source to show. The two diagrams below are from the design documents behind it.

media.caption: What is live. Two Savi products share one core: prompts and guidelines, the knowledge base, the answer composer and a trace of every request, with the learning loop running from reported outcomes to human review.

Where it is headed. New products connect the same way with no new plumbing, proposed rule changes are backtested against history before review, and an MCP front door lets internal tools and agents reach the knowledge base directly.

projects.name: Savi Assistant
projects.blurb: Client-facing AI assistant for Savi. Retrieval over the help centre, streamed replies, and tool calling.
projects.details:
Built for Savi as their main client-facing assistant. Help centre content is chunked out of PDFs, embedded, and indexed in a vector database, so answers are retrieved by meaning rather than keyword match. Replies stream to the browser over Server-Sent Events, and the model can call tools to act rather than only answer. Built on the Laravel AI SDK against the Anthropic API. The retrieval approach is the same cosine-similarity technique behind Gem's memory system, pointed at a different corpus.

The clip below is the live assistant answering a repayment question: it searches the help centre first, then streams the answer.

media.caption: Asking it what RAP is. The assistant searches the help centre before answering, then streams the reply over Server-Sent Events; the search step shows while the tool call runs.

projects.name: Gem
projects.blurb: Fully self-hosted household AI assistant. Three repos, a dual-GPU box in the house, one Flutter codebase across Android, iOS, iPad and web, and a memory system that metabolises conversations while nobody is looking.
projects.details:
*Scroll down for screencaps of Gem in action.*

Gem is the AI assistant my household actually uses. She runs on a machine in my house and answers on a phone, a browser, and an iPad mounted in the kitchen. Three repositories: a FastAPI server, one Flutter client covering Android, iOS, iPad and web, and an infrastructure repo for the box.

**The machine.** A dual-GPU Ubuntu box. The AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32GB) runs the 31B conversation model; the NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12GB) runs embeddings, speech and a small utility model. One Ollama process cannot split a model across mixed AMD and NVIDIA silicon, so each card runs its own instance and a model string can name which one serves it. Nothing leaves the house except web search.

**What she can do**

- Web search, weather and timers
- Reminders and recurring tasks that fire on wall-clock time
- Shared household lists
- Notes you write, and Memories she writes herself
- A news feed whose search queries she picks from what she knows about each person
- Read-only calendar sync from subscribed ICS feeds
- Plaid transaction sync
- Spotify, with the box as the house's Bluetooth speaker and its levels driving the console's visualiser
- Most of these dock as mini apps inside the chat, plus Android home-screen widgets

**Memory.** Every note lives in three places kept in sync: a flat markdown vault, MySQL for ownership and tags, and a Qdrant point for the embedding. A note is owned by one or more people and carries tags rather than sitting in a folder, and ownership is the entire access check. An idle loop distils conversations into atomic notes and audits the whole store on a longer cadence, freezing the moment anyone reconnects so the GPU is free before their message arrives.

**Retrieval.** A question is embedded once, and that same vector is matched against a separate collection of tag-name embeddings; confident tags become a hard filter before cosine similarity runs inside the narrowed subset, so choosing them costs no extra model call. Every answer leaves a forensic trace: the query with every vector hit and score, each tool's arguments and result, and the exact prompt sent to the model.

**Who is talking.** The kitchen iPad is shared, so "what's on my list" has to know whose. SpeechBrain speaker embeddings match each sentence against a person's enrolled voice, and a confident match returns a short-lived token for them, so the prompt, the retrieval and every tool are already scoped to the right person. Only the embedding is stored, never the audio.

**The console.** The same Flutter codebase in a different mode: an ambient face showing weather, the day's agenda and a voice visualiser. "Hey Gem" is caught on-device by an ONNX classifier trained on recordings of the household. She sleeps after a minute of quiet and wakes on the wake word, a touch, or motion — read from the front camera as a coarse brightness grid, no frame kept, and armed only while she is asleep.

In daily use at home, shipped to real devices through Firebase App Distribution.

media.caption: The kitchen console. Ambient weather, the day's agenda and a voice visualiser; it sleeps after a minute and wakes on "hey Gem", a touch, or motion.
Memories: the notes the idle loop wrote from conversations, tagged and vector-indexed. A person can edit one but never creates one.
Notes are the other half of the same tables: a person's own scratchpad, never embedded and invisible to the audit, so Gem cannot silently rewrite one.
Web search. The conversation model decides for itself that a question is time-sensitive enough to need it, then answers from what came back.
Weather, from a free geocoding and forecast API. The location argument is optional and falls back to a household setting when the model leaves it out.
Shared lists, docked as a mini app inside the chat rather than a separate screen.
Calendar. Events sync read-only from subscribed ICS feeds, so they are editable at the source and nowhere else.

projects.name: Pip
projects.blurb: The predecessor to Gem. An OpenAI-backed assistant living on a Raspberry Pi with a 3 inch display, in a 3D-printed case mounted on the kitchen wall.
projects.details:
Pip was the first attempt at the idea Gem now does properly, and the first attempt at embedded AI: a household assistant that is a physical object rather than an app. A Raspberry Pi behind a 3 inch display, in a case he designed and printed for it, bolted to the kitchen wall with a camera and a shotgun microphone above it. Idle, it showed a pair of eyes with the temperature and time; spoken to, it answered through the OpenAI API.

Two repositories: a Python backend and a separate frontend for the display, both running in Docker on the Pi. Everything Gem got right about being local and owned came out of what Pip got wrong by depending on somebody else's API.

media.caption: Mounted on the kitchen wall, camera and microphone above the display.
The 3D-printed case from another angle.
The display on the bench during the build, showing the idle eyes, temperature and time.

projects.name: VectorCloud
projects.blurb: His first open source project: a web interface for the Anki Vector robot, built the month Vector shipped and officially adopted by Anki.
projects.details:
Anki released Vector in the autumn of 2018 and Ross bought one straight away. Within weeks he had written VectorCloud: a self-hosted web interface and control surface for the robot, built in Python and Flask on top of Vector's SDK, so you could drive it, watch what it saw and run behaviours from a browser on the same network. It was the first thing he ever published.

Anki adopted it officially, which is the part worth noting: an open source side project picked up by the hardware manufacturer whose product it extended. It gathered 124 GitHub stars and 19 forks and ran in Docker from the start. Development stopped when Anki shut down in 2019 and took the robot's future with it.

It set the pattern for everything since. Open source, self-hosted, a piece of hardware in the room made more useful by software around it.

media.caption: VectorCloud connected to a Vector on the home network. A command bar for the robot, an application store for packages built on the SDK, and the robot's own details reported back: OS 1.3, SDK 0.5.1, the state of the art in 2018.

projects.name: This site
projects.blurb: Flutter web on S3 and CloudFront, FastAPI on ECS Fargate, all defined in CDK and shipped by GitHub Actions. The assistant you are talking to runs on Bedrock embeddings and a Qdrant collection of this record.
projects.details:
The diagram below is the whole thing. One CloudFront distribution fronts two origins: the default behaviour serves the Flutter bundle out of a private S3 bucket over Origin Access Control, and /api/* goes to an Application Load Balancer in front of a FastAPI task on ECS Fargate. Because both live behind the same distribution the browser is same-origin with the API, so there is no CORS anywhere. The load balancer's security group admits only CloudFront's origin-facing prefix list, which means api.mountjoy.io cannot be reached directly even though it has a public certificate.

The VPC has no NAT gateway. Tasks sit in public subnets with a public IP and reach S3 and DynamoDB over gateway endpoints, which costs nothing, rather than paying for a managed NAT to do the same work.

All of it is AWS CDK in Python, split into four stacks so the stateful pieces can carry termination protection and RETAIN policies while the compute and edge stacks stay disposable. GitHub Actions deploys on every push to main through OIDC federation, so there are no AWS keys stored anywhere in the repo or in GitHub. DynamoDB is a single table holding rate-limit counters keyed by a salted hash of the caller's IP, with a TTL so old rows expire themselves.

The assistant is Claude with a system prompt built from this same profile record. Portfolio content is embedded with Amazon Bedrock Titan and indexed in Qdrant, which both retrieves context for answers and drives the interactive graph you get from /projects. The system prompt is assembled once at import so the cached prefix stays byte-identical between requests and prompt caching actually hits; retrieved excerpts go into the user turn instead, where they cannot break the cache.

Source is public.

media.caption: Production architecture. One CloudFront distribution fronts both the S3 bundle and the Fargate API, so the browser is same-origin with the API. The load balancer only admits the CloudFront prefix list.

projects.name: Pi Game Boy
projects.blurb: A hardware build from 2017: a handheld console with a 3D-printed case and buttons, Adafruit boards soldered together by hand, a Raspberry Pi running RetroPie, and HDMI out to the TV.
projects.details:
Before any of the software, hardware. This is the electronics, soldering and 3D-printing side of the record. In 2017 I built a Game Boy from parts: a Raspberry Pi for the computer, Adafruit's PiTFT display and PiGRRL gamepad board, a PowerBoost charger and a LiPo cell for battery power, a small speaker with an amp, and a case and every button designed and 3D-printed to fit them. Everything is soldered by hand, including the gamepad matrix and the wiring between the boards.

It runs RetroPie, the Linux distribution for emulation, on the Pi. The case exposes the Pi's ports rather than hiding them, so it takes a full-size HDMI cable, a headphone jack, USB and Ethernet. Plug it into a television and it becomes a console: the handheld's screen goes to the TV and a controller goes into a USB port.

It was the first thing I built where the software was the easy part. Getting a battery, a charge circuit, a display, a speaker and thirteen buttons to share a case the size of the original meant learning the hardware end to end, and it is the same instinct that later put Pip on the kitchen wall and Gem on an iPad in the kitchen.

media.caption: The finished unit. Every button and the case itself came off the printer.

Plugged into the television over HDMI, with a controller in a USB port. RetroPie's menu on the big screen, the handheld on the table.

Side cutouts for the headphone jack and full-size HDMI.
USB and Ethernet exposed at the top rather than sealed in, so it doubles as a console.
